clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant condition within the PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome spectrum, caused by germline loss-of-function variants in the PTEN tumour-suppressor gene
Characterised by multiple hamartomas across skin, mucosa, breast, thyroid, endometrium and gastrointestinal tract
Mucocutaneous features include trichilemmomas, oral papillomas (cobblestone mucosa) and acral/palmoplantar keratoses
Macrocephaly is a common and clinically useful clue, and dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte-Duclos disease) is a characteristic association
There is a markedly increased lifetime risk of breast, thyroid (usually follicular or papillary), endometrial and renal cancers
PTEN is a key negative regulator of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, so its loss drives excessive cell growth and survival
Management centres on intensified organ-specific cancer surveillance beginning in early adulthood, and earlier for thyroid assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Cowden syndrome is caused by germline inactivating variants in PTEN, a tumour-suppressor gene encoding a phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3 and thereby restrains the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mTOR signalling axis. Loss of PTEN function removes this brake, leading to constitutive pathway activation that promotes cell growth, proliferation and survival. This drives the widespread hamartomatous overgrowth and elevated cancer risk across multiple organs. The syndrome sits within the broader PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome spectrum, which also includes Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome and related phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis with gastrointestinal hamartomas
Multiple endocrine neoplasia with thyroid involvement
Familial breast or thyroid cancer without a hamartoma syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Germline molecular genetic testing of PTEN including deletion/duplication analysis
Breast imaging surveillance in women per guidelines
Thyroid ultrasound and clinical thyroid assessment from a young age
Endometrial surveillance and prompt evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding
Colonoscopy for gastrointestinal polyps and renal imaging for renal cancer
Brain MRI when Lhermitte-Duclos disease or neurological symptoms are suspected
redFlags: New breast lump or abnormal breast imaging in an affected individual
Thyroid nodule with suspicious features suggesting carcinoma
Postmenopausal or abnormal uterine bleeding raising concern for endometrial cancer
Progressive headache, ataxia or raised intracranial pressure suggesting Lhermitte-Duclos disease
reference.prognosis: With adherence to intensified surveillance many cancers can be detected early, but the substantial cumulative lifetime risk of breast, thyroid and endometrial malignancy means long-term outcome depends on sustained monitoring. Benign hamartomas contribute to symptom burden but are rarely life-threatening.
pitfalls: Overlooking macrocephaly and mucocutaneous features that should prompt PTEN testing
Failing to start thyroid surveillance in childhood when indicated
Attributing gastrointestinal polyps or skin lesions to unrelated common conditions
Not extending cancer surveillance and genetic testing to at-risk relatives
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Intensified lifelong cancer surveillance across affected organs, as there is no specific drug therapy for the underlying PTEN loss
Breast surveillance with clinical examination and imaging including MRI in women, with consideration of risk-reducing mastectomy
Thyroid ultrasound surveillance from a young age, with thyroidectomy for malignancy
Endometrial surveillance and prompt evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding, with consideration of risk-reducing hysterectomy
Colonoscopic surveillance for gastrointestinal polyps and renal imaging for renal cell carcinoma
Excision or topical treatment of symptomatic mucocutaneous hamartomas, and brain MRI for suspected Lhermitte-Duclos disease
Consider mTOR pathway inhibition such as sirolimus for troublesome overgrowth manifestations under specialist or trial settings
Genetic counselling with PTEN testing and cascade screening of at-risk relatives
